did_you_know.text: Did you know? After Haman’s downfall, the king gave Esther Haman’s estate, and Mordecai was brought before the king after Esther told him how he was related to her.
Did you know? The king removed his royal ring—the symbol of authority—from Haman and gave it to Mordecai; Esther also placed Mordecai in charge of Haman’s estate.

Did you know? Esther was not satisfied merely with saving Mordecai and receiving Haman’s estate; she continued to plead with the king to overturn the evil plotted by Haman and his plan against the Jews.
Did you know? When Esther fell at the king’s feet, he extended the golden scepter toward her, and she rose and stood before him.

Did you know? According to the king’s decree, a document written in the king’s name and sealed with his ring could not be revoked; therefore, a new decree was written allowing the Jews to defend themselves.

Did you know? The new decree was written on the twenty-third day of Sivan, the third month, and sent to 127 provinces—from India to Cush—to every people in its own language and every province in its own script.
Did you know? The letters were written in the king’s name, sealed with the king’s ring, and sent by couriers riding swift horses from the royal stables.
Did you know? The decree gave the Jews permission to assemble and defend themselves against their enemies on the appointed day, the thirteenth day of Adar.
Did you know? Mordecai left the king’s presence wearing royal garments of blue, white linen, and purple, along with a large golden crown; as a result, the city of Susa rejoiced and celebrated.
Did you know? The chapter describes the Jews’ joy in four words: “light, gladness, joy, and honor.”
Did you know? Wherever the king’s decree reached, the Jews rejoiced, held a feast, and celebrated; many people of the land “became Jews” because fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.
